title: Scientists Calculated the Exact Sleep Window That Slows Ageing. It Is Not Eight Hours.
excerpt: A study of half a million people published in Nature found that sleeping between 6.4 and 7.8 hours a night produced the youngest biological age across nearly every organ. For South Asians who sleep too little or too much, the findings are a wake-up call.
body:
Eight hours of sleep has been gospel for decades. A massive new study says the science no longer supports it.

Researchers at Columbia University analysed data from nearly 500,000 adults in the UK Biobank — the world's largest repository of health, lifestyle, and biological data — and found that the biological aging sweet spot falls between 6.4 and 7.8 hours of sleep per night. People who slept within that range had the youngest-looking bodies, as measured by machine-learning-derived 'ageing clocks' that estimate how old individual organs really are compared to a person's chronological age.

The study, published in Nature, found that too little sleep — under six hours — was significantly associated with depressive episodes, anxiety disorders, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and obesity. But too much sleep was also a problem. People getting more than eight hours showed signs of faster biological ageing, and those with both short and long sleep patterns were more likely to develop asthma and digestive disorders.

## How the Ageing Clocks Work

The research uses an emerging field of biomarkers known as biological ageing clocks. Instead of measuring chronological age, these tools use hundreds of biomarkers to calculate how fast specific organs are ageing. A 50-year-old with a sedentary lifestyle and poor sleep might have a heart that functions like a 60-year-old's and lungs that test like a 55-year-old's.

"Our study shows that too little and too much sleep are associated with faster aging in nearly every organ," said lead author Junhao Wen, an assistant professor of radiology at Columbia University. "Sleep may speed aging in the brain, heart, lung, and immune system — and is associated with a wide range of diseases."

The research goes beyond the familiar advice to simply sleep more. What makes this study significant is that it identifies a specific range and links deviation from it to measurable organ-level ageing — not just next-day tiredness, but long-term biological decline.

## A Second Study Adds Weight

Separate research presented at the SLEEP 2026 annual meeting reinforces the Columbia findings from a different angle. A National Sleep Foundation study found that adults who feel older than their chronological age consistently report worse sleep outcomes — more insomnia symptoms, less regular sleep, and greater daytime impairment. The relationship between feeling old and sleeping poorly persisted even after accounting for depression, anxiety, and actual chronological age.

"Adults who felt older than their actual age consistently reported poorer sleep outcomes," said Joseph Dzierzewski, the principal investigator and senior vice president of research at the National Sleep Foundation. The study found that this mismatch between subjective and actual age predicted poorer physical health, mediated through the sleep disruption itself.

In other words, a vicious cycle may be at play. Poor sleep makes you feel older. Feeling older worsens your sleep. And both accelerate biological ageing.

## The South Asian Sleep Problem

These findings land differently for the Indian diaspora. Studies consistently show that South Asians in the US and UK sleep less than their white counterparts, driven by a combination of cultural factors, work patterns, and health conditions. The 'hustle culture' common in many immigrant households often treats sleep as optional. Late nights are a badge of honour in many Indian families.

The Columbia study suggests this is not just a quality-of-life issue. Chronic short sleep is measurably ageing your organs faster. For a community already at elevated risk for cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome — conditions where organ ageing plays a central role — the implications are serious.

The research also matters for ageing parents. Many older South Asians report sleeping nine or more hours but still feeling tired. The UK Biobank data suggests this pattern of long, poor-quality sleep may be accelerating ageing rather than supporting recovery.

## What to Do With This

The practical guidance is narrow and specific. Aim for 6.4 to 7.8 hours of actual sleep, not time in bed. Regularity matters as much as duration — the SLEEP 2026 data shows that irregular sleep schedules independently predict worse outcomes.

For NRIs managing demanding careers and family obligations across time zones, this means making sleep a non-negotiable rather than a variable. A late-night call with family in India followed by a 6 AM start is precisely the kind of pattern the data says will age your body faster than your years.

The encouraging finding is that sleep is modifiable. Unlike your genetics or your childhood nutrition, your sleep schedule is something you can change tonight. The science says the window is narrower than most people assume, and both ends of the spectrum carry risk. Getting it right may be one of the most straightforward things you can do to slow biological ageing.
